Fugitives
fū'jĭ-tĭvz
n. pl. (those who flee; refugees, deserters, or escapees, according to context)
Latin fugitivus, from fugere, to flee. The word carries both pity and reproach in Scripture, and the two are seldom far apart.

Biblical Definition

The word is first an insult. The men of Ephraim, quarrelling with Gilead after Jephthah's victory, taunted them: “Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim among the Ephraimites, and among the Manassites” (Jdg 12:4) — a slur about ancestry and belonging that ended in forty-two thousand Ephraimites dead at the fords of Jordan over the pronunciation of one word. Then it is a category of judgment: at the fall of Jerusalem, “the fugitives that fell away to the king of Babylon” were carried away by Nebuzaradan with the rest (2Ki 25:11) — deserting to the winning side did not save them. Then it is an object of pity: “My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar” (Isa 15:5), and the prophet who pronounces the burden of Moab weeps over it. And finally it is a sentence: “all his fugitives with all his bands shall fall by the sword” (Eze 17:21), on Zedekiah who broke his oath to Babylon. Scripture's attitude toward the man in flight is therefore never simple, and the law had already settled the practical question long before: the cities of refuge stood open, and the escaped servant was not to be delivered up to his master.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a fugitive as one who flees from danger, pursuit, duty or service; a deserter; one who has fled or escaped from his country.

expand to see more

FUGITIVE, n. One who flees from his station or duty; a deserter; one who flees from danger.

2. One who has fled or deserted and taken refuge under another power, or one who has fled from punishment.

3. One hard to be caught or detained; that which is fleeting and unstable.

Key Scripture

Jdg 12:4 — "Then Jephthah gathered together all the men of Gilead, and fought with Ephraim: and the men of Gilead smote Ephraim, because they said, Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim among the Ephraimites, and among the Manassites."

Isa 15:5 — "My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction."

Deu 23:15 — "Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped from his master unto thee:"

Modern Corruption

Scripture's treatment of the man in flight is regularly flattened into one policy or another, when the Bible gives a settled duty toward the fleeing and a settled refusal to make his flight a proof of innocence.

expand to see more

The Bible speaks about fugitives more often than most readers realise, and it never speaks in one register. There is a plain duty of refuge: the escaped servant is not to be handed back but is to dwell where it liketh him best, and thou shalt not oppress him (Deu 23:15-16); six cities stood open across the land for the man who had killed unawares; the stranger within the gates is protected in the law again and again, and Israel is told why — ye were strangers in the land of Egypt. And there is an equally plain refusal to treat flight as a verdict: the cities of refuge held a trial, and the manslayer who proved to be a murderer was delivered up to the avenger of blood. Zedekiah's fugitives fled from an oath he had sworn by God. The modern discussion tends to collapse this into a single posture — either that every fleeing person is by definition innocent and owed everything, or that the fleeing are by definition guilty and owed nothing. Scripture holds both duties without embarrassment: shelter the fugitive, and judge the case. Isaiah 15 shows the temper the church should have while doing it, and it is not neutrality. The prophet announcing Moab's destruction says, My heart shall cry out for Moab.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew paliyt (H6412), an escaped one, a fugitive; naphal (H5307), to fall away, to desert; miqlat (H4733), a refuge, the cities of refuge.

expand to see more

Hebrew paliyt (H6412) — an escaped one, a fugitive; used of the man who brought Abram word, and of Moab's refugees; Genesis 14:13, Isaiah 15:5.

Hebrew naphal (H5307) — to fall, and idiomatically to fall away or desert to an enemy; the fugitives that fell away to Babylon; 2 Kings 25:11, Jeremiah 39:9.

Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a refuge, an asylum; the six cities appointed for the man who fled; Numbers 35:11, Joshua 20:2.

Usage

"“Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim” — a slur about belonging that cost forty-two thousand lives."

"“His fugitives shall flee unto Zoar” — the prophet weeping over the nation he condemns."

"“Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped” — the law of refuge."
